title: Many Reformers: calling assurance an act of faith does not equalize it with 'Christ is God's Son'
source_text: CXXXVIII. Patet igitur, secundum expressam Reformatorum multorum doctrinam, inter ea quae ad fidem pertinent, varios esse certitudinis gradus, quoniam fides eorum respectu, non eodem modo se habet. Sunt enim quaedam circa quae assensus noster unice & immediate nititur divina revelatione: alia vero circa quae partim divina revelatione, partim alius generis mediis atque argumentis nititur; cujusmodi sunt conclusiones ex una propositione revelata deductae, & ex altera, quae vel fama constanti, vel rationis lumine, vel sensuum tum externorum, tum internorum experientia, cognita nobis & manifesta est. Et haec & illa ad fidem referuntur, & assensus uterque pro actu fidei apud Reformatos habetur. Verumtamen in utrisque, ex eorundem Reformatorum sensu, par firmitas & certitudo non est: sed maxima in iis quae sola revelatione nituntur; in aliis vero major vel minor pro proportione certitudinis & evidentiae, quae inest propositioni, quae revelatae adjungitur, ut ex ea haec vel illa conclusio deducatur, sicut jam exposueram, in Thesibus quas reprehendit vir doctus: idque non solum ex mea privata, sed ex plurium Scholae Reformatae Doctorum aperta sententia. Unde apparet quam vana sit illius probatio, dum ex eo quod Reformati actum fidei vocant, persuasionem illam, quam vere fidelis & justus habet de propria gratia & remissione peccatorum suorum, colligit secundum communem Reformatorum sententiam, unumquemque fidelem, pari cum certitudine & firmitate persuasum esse de remissione peccatorum suorum, ac est de eo quod Christus est Dei filius & mundi Redemptor.
pass_a_gloss: It is clear therefore, according to the express doctrine of many of the Reformers, that among those things which pertain to faith there are various degrees of certainty, because faith does not stand in the same way with respect to them. For there are certain things around which our assent rests uniquely and immediately upon divine revelation: but others around which it rests partly upon divine revelation, partly upon means and arguments of another kind; of which sort are conclusions deduced from one revealed proposition and from another which is known and manifest to us either by constant report, or by the light of reason, or by the experience of the senses both external and internal. And both these and those are referred to faith, and either assent is held among the Reformed as an act of faith. Nevertheless in both, according to the sense of the same Reformers, there is not equal firmness and certainty: but the greatest in those which rest on revelation alone; in the others greater or lesser in proportion to the certainty and evidence which is in the proposition that is joined to the revealed one, so that from it this or that conclusion may be deduced — as I had already set out in the Theses which the learned man reprehends: and that not only from my private judgment, but from the open sentence of many Doctors of the Reformed School. Whence appears how vain is his proof, when from this — that the Reformed call an act of faith that persuasion which the truly faithful and just man has concerning his own grace and the remission of his sins — he gathers that according to the common judgment of the Reformers each faithful person is persuaded with equal certainty and firmness concerning the remission of his sins as he is concerning this, that Christ is the Son of God and Redeemer of the world.
pass_b_english: Many Reformers expressly teach graded certainty within faith: some assents rest on revelation alone; others mix revelation with report, reason, or sensory experience — yet both count as acts of faith.

Equal firmness does not follow: maximum certainty belongs to revelation-alone articles; mixed conclusions vary with the weaker premise — as Le Blanc already taught, and many Reformed doctors openly say.
So calling own-grace persuasion an act of faith does not prove common Reformed consent that it matches certainty that Christ is God's Son and the world's Redeemer.
